en: Your dear mother Kanykei
Carried him without rest for nine months,
As though she herself had borne him.
Had you heeded my words before,
Külchoro, who drank the right breast,
Would have been your inheritance,
A loyal follower of your good counsel;
But your Kanchoro, who drank the left breast,
Is in his heart your enemy—
He appears a foe to my eyes.
Take care, my child, and hear my words:
If you continue raising Kanchoro,
He will become your calamity.
His enmity is revealed,
For from my breast, my foal,
Black blood flows and pours;
At heart he appears an enemy.
If sent against a foe, he will not support you;
Let the wretch go his way—
At heart he will never be your ally.
He is an unripe cucumber and will never grow sharp;
The first omen has appeared:
He is a calamity and will never form a loyal people.
If he lives and grows,
He will mature into a warrior,
Become the equal of heroic sons,
And answer your words with defiance;
Claiming to be your brother, he will fire his gun
And become your enemy.
He will sow discord among your people;
When you confront a battling foe,
He will blacken your face with shame,
Make hollows of your open eyes,
And bring your death upon you.
If this Choro survives,
He will strip you of your honor.
His faith is alien,
And at heart he is your enemy.
Your radiant father had the habit
Of treating his ancestral foes like brothers,
Pitying them as kin,
And so he would die
At the hands of those closest to him.
Find a brother from another place
And make him your support, she said;
This child is not your brother—
Finish him off, she said.
But I would not heed my mother;
Thinking, ‘What can one lone son do?’
I did not keep him apart from my equals.
And now, at the final hour,
This bastard Kanchoro
Has proved an enemy at heart.
My enemy became my brother,
My foe dwelt at my very heart.
Did I go about calling Kanchoro and Külchoro
My brothers?
Has my poor soul flared and burned,
Consumed by one close to me?
Those were the words my mother planted;
She said he had always been an enemy.
When my blessed mother Kanykei
Spoke with care, I disobeyed,
Unable to foresee my death—
And now I am doomed to die miserably.
My own Kanchoro has become my foe;
Grieving and enduring affliction,
Deprived of my gray horse,
With not a blade of grass to nibble,
Not a sip of water to swallow,
I am doomed to die in the desert.
With no famed enemy to blame,
I am doomed to die among my own people;
With mist covering the earth,
I am doomed to be left upon the pass,
Burning and blazing here,
Abandoned in the wilderness.
My valiant mother Kanykei
Had warned me with anguished cries:
‘At heart, Kanchoro
Will recite the prophecies you sang,
Reveal your secrets to the enemy,
And join them in bringing about your end;
All your nurturing of him is in vain.
Will he reveal the foe within his heart
And abandon you?
Will he begin
A terrible affliction and great strife?
When you see his monstrous deceit,
You will blaze and burn like fire,
And then you will know
That your poor mother spoke the truth.
You will know the great prophetic gift
Of your hapless, valiant mother,
That sacred, unfortunate woman.’
Those were my mother’s words;
She said he was an enemy at heart.
Her prophecy has come true—
My fierce, mighty mother’s
Words, my foal, have proved true.
My dear mother Kanykei,
When he was still an infant,
Before he had begun to grow,
Told me to cut off his head with a sword,
To finish him off;
She said it not once, but a thousand times.
So I was fated to witness
This musket-tailed villainy;
So I was fated to die
At the hands of a close kinsman and warrior.
Shamed despite my swift racing stallion,
Abused by my own kin,
I am doomed to die a wretched death,
Burning to ashes and embers,
Doomed to die an unclean death.
Damn you, Kanchoro!
My Külchoro and my Kanchoro,
My two nest-mates, my equal warriors—
Yesterday, on the plain of Jylgynduu,
Along the broad Talas,
In the marshes of Jylgynduu and Keng-Kol,
When we reveled in delight,
If anyone laid hands upon your horses,
Though he said, ‘That is my only horse,’
We would slaughter it and eat it.
If my two lions remained loyal,
We said, where could calamity come from?
Did God hear our arrogant boast?
Has the gasping enemy
Who tears out lungs and severs heads
Sprung from my own hearth?”
So Semetey spoke,
Leaning upon
His golden-bladed battle-axe;
Grieving, he folded his hands,
His heart filled with bitter anguish,
And the gray wolf stood lamenting.
Your hero, renowned as a hero,
Shed tears from his dear falcon eyes
Without even turning them aside.
His heart burned and his eyes blazed;
His poor soul could not be contained in a fist,
And he seethed in torment.
What is here today is gone tomorrow;
His heart was aflame, his breast an ember.
When the low ebb of fate arrives,
Is it always so faithless?
Damn this worthless world!
His heart was aflame, his soul an ember,
And he had no charger to ride to war.
Unable to contain his grief,
Semetey wailed aloud.
Allah’s sun in the heavens grew dark,
And sixty afflictions at once
Descended upon the noble lion’s head.
The layers of his ribs split apart,
And his wretched heart was torn;
The enmity of Chubak’s son Choro
Stood revealed.
Straining and gathering his force,
Your gray wolf fell into true despair
And lost all hope of his tiny soul.
Unable to collect his thoughts,
The lion-hearted gray wolf was distraught;
Before the votive meat was even cooked,
He suffered grievous tribulation.
The dear lion of a man
Put on his Akolpok armor,
Despairing of his borrowed life;
He strode heavily, bracing himself,
Leaning upon his Akkelte,
Slung his musket over his shoulder,
Prayed to the Creator,
And prepared his weapons.
He buckled on his scabbardless sword,
While wrath swept across his face
Like a storm cloud returning.
Thick-wristed and peerless,
Unlike ordinary mortals in appearance,
He had received letters from many lands
And blessings from holy fathers;
The Twelve had joined hands as one
And named him to become a lion.
He was that lion who never turned,
That warrior who never faltered.
He was his father’s true son,
That fathomless black gray wolf.
The offspring of one who grieved at ease
And smiled at hardship,
He rejoiced when told he would die—
Thus was his lionheartedness known.
He made the white doe his home,
Made those who shot at him his prey,
Chased the blue doe and made it cattle,
And made every land he sought his own.
He was both champion and lion.
He was a matchless warrior;
Having created this gray wolf,
God would never grant his like again.
His fortune was complete,
And the bloodthirsty hero’s heart
Was broader than the face of the earth.
He spared no foe who grappled with him;
In all the eighteen thousand worlds,
No one remained
Who would cast a lasso at the mighty gray wolf.
His courage was extraordinary,
His strength beyond measure.
Now grieving in anguish,
He whose learning was the lesson of the Qur’an,
Whose gray horse had been his wings,
Grieved in sorrow;
Deprived of Arbuurul,
The dear lion who never flinched,
Whom God had fashioned supreme,
The renowned hero favored by holy powers,
Grew wary of Kanchoro
And saddled Artoru.
Fourteen horses had come from Talas,
All fourteen swift thoroughbreds,
Broad-chested and low-maned,
Well-proportioned chargers,
Their lower legs as thick as a child’s waist;
The strides of the dark steeds
Were like the winter wind across the uplands.
Their splayed hooves were broad as Chatkal;
Upon the bones where three joints met,
A twelve-handled cauldron
Could seemingly be hung.
Broad-bellied and wide-backed,
Peerless Artoru—
Such was Artoru’s nature.
The bay belonged to gray wolf Semetey;
This was the bloodthirsty hero’s heavenly steed,
The horse he rode into battle
After Arbuurul.
He saddled Artoru,
Fearing for his borrowed life,
Buckled on Zulpukor,
And readied Akkelte.
He tied the sacred gray pouch
Around his waist,
But it gave no sign.
Formerly, when the bloodthirsty leopard
Tied the gray pouch at his waist,
The Forty Chiltens and Kyzır Niyaz
Would form forty thousand troops,
Advancing from the ridges;
They became forty thousand men against the foe,
Rising from the earth as an army—
The heart of anyone who saw them would fail.
Such was their protection.
Dividing into countless hosts,
They would join him and level their spears;
The Forty Chiltens, united as companions,
Would raise their battle cry.
